fields_at_offsets.name: LegacyVersion
fields_at_offsets.value: 0x0301 (TLS 1.0 for backwards compat; real version negotiated in extensions)

explanation: TLS 1.3 wire format keeps record-layer ContentType=0x16 (Handshake) and uses legacy versions 0x0301/0x0303 in two places for middlebox-compatibility. The real protocol version is announced via the supported_versions extension. Identifying TLS 1.3 vs TLS 1.2 from the wire requires parsing extensions, not the legacy version field. Common analyst question: 'is this connection TLS 1.3?' - the answer requires looking inside extensions for type 0x002b with value 0x0304.

The SNI extension lets a TLS client tell the server which hostname it wants to connect to before the handshake completes - required for virtual hosting where multiple TLS sites share an IP. SNI is ALSO sent in cleartext in TLS 1.0-1.2 and (by default) TLS 1.3, making it the primary signal for L4-firewall HTTPS filtering. Encrypted ClientHello (ECH) is the extension that finally encrypts SNI, but it's still rare in practice. Analyst use: SNI tells you which domain a TLS connection is going to, even if you can't decrypt the rest.

fields_at_offsets.name: ContentType
fields_at_offsets.value: 0x17 (ApplicationData; in TLS 1.3 every post-handshake record uses this even for handshake messages)

explanation: After the TLS handshake completes, every record uses ContentType=0x17 (ApplicationData) regardless of the inner content - this is a TLS 1.3 privacy improvement that hides handshake-vs-data distinction from passive observers. The actual content type lives inside the encrypted blob. Analyst implication: in TLS 1.3 you cannot tell from the wire whether a record carries application data, alerts, or post-handshake messages without decrypting.

DNS wire format is compact. Key fields for analysts: TransactionID (used to match query<->response and detect spoofing), Flags (the 0x0100 standard query bit pattern), and QNAME (the queried domain in length-prefixed label form, NOT a null-terminated string). DNS tunneling shows up as queries with very long QNAME labels carrying base64-encoded data; recognising the wire format is the first step to detecting that.

fields_at_offsets.name: Name
fields_at_offsets.value: 0xC00C (compression pointer to offset 0x0C in the message - the QNAME)

explanation: DNS responses use name compression (0xC0 byte high two bits set, then 14-bit offset) to avoid repeating the QNAME in every answer record. RDATA format depends on TYPE: A records carry 4 bytes of IPv4, AAAA carries 16 bytes IPv6, CNAME carries a name in label format. Reading DNS by hand requires tracking the message-relative offsets that compression pointers refer to.

HTTP/2 wire format: 9-byte frame header followed by Length bytes of payload. Frame types: 0x00 DATA, 0x01 HEADERS, 0x04 SETTINGS, 0x05 PUSH_PROMISE, 0x06 PING, 0x07 GOAWAY, 0x08 WINDOW_UPDATE. Stream IDs: client-initiated are odd, server-initiated even, 0 is connection-level. HTTP/2 request smuggling attacks abuse the framing by sending crafted headers that the front-end and back-end interpret differently; recognising the frame structure is the first step to spotting smuggling traffic.

hex_pattern: FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF 00 5C 02 00 00 00 4D 40 01 01 00 40 02 06 02 01 00 00 FB FF 40 03 04 C0 A8 01 01 80 04 04 00 00 00 00

fields_at_offsets.name: Marker
fields_at_offsets.value: 16 bytes 0xFF (legacy authentication; always all-ones in BGPv4)

fields_at_offsets.name: AS_PATH attribute
fields_at_offsets.value: type 0x40 0x02, contains a sequence of AS numbers

fields_at_offsets.name: NEXT_HOP attribute
fields_at_offsets.value: type 0x40 0x03, IPv4 address of the next-hop router

explanation: BGP UPDATE messages announce or withdraw IP prefixes. The 16-byte all-ones marker is a BGPv4 holdover from earlier versions that used it for MD5 authentication. Analyst-relevant attributes: AS_PATH (for hijack detection - unexpected ASNs in the path indicate route hijacking), ORIGIN (IGP/EGP/incomplete), NEXT_HOP (where to send traffic), and COMMUNITIES (operator-defined tags). BGP hijacks like the Pakistan-blocks-YouTube incident in 2008 show up as unexpected AS_PATH values.

fields_at_offsets.name: Checksum
fields_at_offsets.value: 0x4D5A (one's complement over the entire ICMP header + data)

fields_at_offsets.name: Data
fields_at_offsets.value: 'Hello' (arbitrary, often used to fingerprint the OS)

explanation: ICMP Echo (ping) is the canonical reachability test. Wire format is simple: 4-byte type/code/checksum, 4-byte identifier+sequence, variable-length data. ICMP tunneling abuses the data field to carry application traffic encapsulated in pings - high-volume Echo Requests with consistent payload size are the signal. ICMP types worth recognising: 0 Echo Reply, 3 Destination Unreachable (with codes 0-15 for reason), 8 Echo Request, 11 Time Exceeded (used by traceroute).

fields_at_offsets.name: Version+IHL
fields_at_offsets.value: 0x45 (high 4 bits: version=4; low 4 bits: header-length=5 dwords = 20 bytes)

explanation: IPv4 header is 20 bytes minimum, more if IHL > 5 (options). TTL is the per-hop decrement field; default values fingerprint the sender's OS (64 = Linux/macOS, 128 = Windows, 255 = Cisco/network gear). Protocol field: 1 ICMP, 6 TCP, 17 UDP, 47 GRE, 50 ESP, 51 AH. Common forensic question: 'where did this packet come from?' answers via SourceIP at offset 0x0C, validated against TTL distance from expected source-to-receiver hop count.

hex_pattern: 01 BB DD 4F 12 34 56 78 9A BC DE F0 50 18 FF FF AB CD 00 00
explanation: TCP header at offset 0x0C carries the flags byte: SYN (0x02), ACK (0x10), FIN (0x01), RST (0x04), PSH (0x08), URG (0x20), ECE (0x40), CWR (0x80). TCP scan signatures show up here: SYN-only is a normal connection attempt, NULL (no flags) and XMAS (FIN|PSH|URG = 0x29) are stealth scans, RST without prior session is post-mortem teardown. Source/destination ports tell you the application: 443 HTTPS, 80 HTTP, 22 SSH, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 3389 RDP, 445 SMB, 3306 MySQL, 5432 PostgreSQL.

Ethernet II wire format: 14-byte header (6 dst MAC, 6 src MAC, 2 EtherType), then payload. EtherType values: 0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x0806 ARP, 0x8100 802.1Q VLAN tag (in which case the real EtherType is at offset 0x10). MAC addresses: first 3 bytes are the OUI (vendor identifier - 00:50:56 VMware, 00:0C:29 VMware, 00:1A:11 Google, etc.), last 3 bytes are device-unique. Spoofed MACs typically have OUIs that don't match the device platform.

fields_at_offsets.name: TargetMAC
fields_at_offsets.value: 00:00:00:00:00:00 (unknown - what the request is asking for)

explanation: ARP resolves IP -> MAC on a local network. The request has TargetMAC zeroed; the reply (opcode 0x0002) fills it in. ARP spoofing attacks send unsolicited replies claiming the gateway's IP belongs to the attacker's MAC, redirecting LAN traffic. Detection: monitor for opcode 0x0002 ARP packets that don't match a recent 0x0001 request, or for sudden IP-MAC pairing changes for the gateway address.

protocol: TLS Certificate (X.509 inside Certificate handshake message)

fields_at_offsets.name: CertificatesLength
fields_at_offsets.value: (3 bytes total length of cert chain)

explanation: TLS Certificate messages carry one or more X.509 certificates in DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) ASN.1 form. Every X.509 cert starts with 0x30 0x82 (or 0x30 0x81 for shorter ones) - the DER SEQUENCE marker. Common analyst tasks: extract the certificate, decode the Subject CN / SAN to identify the server identity, check the issuer chain. The rich structure inside (validity dates, public key, extensions) is the bulk of the bytes.

DHCP wraps BOOTP with a magic cookie 0x63825363 followed by TLV options. Message types via option 53: 1 DISCOVER, 2 OFFER, 3 REQUEST, 4 DECLINE, 5 ACK, 6 NAK, 7 RELEASE, 8 INFORM. Rogue DHCP server attacks show up as OFFER/ACK messages from unauthorised IPs giving clients attacker-controlled DNS / gateway settings. Detection: snoop DHCP and alert on OFFER from non-allowlisted servers.

SMB2/3 protocol id is 0xFE53 'SMB'. SMB1 (deprecated, used by EternalBlue / WannaCry) used 0xFF53 'SMB'. Commands: 0x00 NEGOTIATE, 0x01 SESSION_SETUP, 0x03 TREE_CONNECT, 0x05 CREATE, 0x06 CLOSE, 0x08 READ, 0x09 WRITE. SMB1 negotiate requests on the wire (look for 0xFF 'SMB' in the first 4 bytes of port 445 traffic) are immediate red flags - modern Windows defaults to SMB3 only and SMB1 is mostly seen in attacks attempting to downgrade or exploit unpatched legacy Windows hosts.

fields_at_offsets.name: TCP-LengthPrefix
fields_at_offsets.value: 0x00000200 (only in TCP-mode Kerberos; UDP omits this)

explanation: Kerberos messages are ASN.1 DER. Message type 10 is AS-REQ (initial authentication), 11 AS-REP, 12 TGS-REQ, 13 TGS-REP, 14 AP-REQ, 15 AP-REP. Pre-authentication failures (KRB5KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED) are the canonical Kerberoasting setup signal - attackers issue TGS-REQs for service principals to harvest service-account password hashes for offline cracking. Detecting unusual ASN.1 message-type frequency is the analyst-side approach.

QUIC runs over UDP (typically port 443) and replaces the TCP+TLS+HTTP/2 stack with a single integrated protocol. The Long header is used during connection establishment; once handshake completes, packets switch to Short header (high bit 0). Connection IDs are how QUIC handles connection migration (changing IPs without dropping the session). QUIC encrypts almost everything including the packet number, so passive observation gives you very little - this is intentionally privacy-preserving and frustrates middlebox-based filtering.

fields_at_offsets.name: Ciphers
fields_at_offsets.value: Hyphen-separated list of cipher suite values from the ClientHello

fields_at_offsets.name: Extensions
fields_at_offsets.value: Hyphen-separated extension type values, in the order they appeared

explanation: JA3 is a fingerprinting technique that hashes the comma-separated string above (in MD5) to identify TLS clients. Different libraries (Chrome, Firefox, curl, python-requests, Cobalt Strike, RedLine stealer) produce distinct JA3 hashes because they enumerate ciphers / extensions / curves in different orders. Defenders use JA3 to detect malware that uses non-browser TLS stacks even when the connection appears benign at the URL level. JA3S is the server-side equivalent based on the ServerHello.

fields_at_offsets.name: ConnectFlags
fields_at_offsets.value: 0x02 (CleanSession bit set; bits 7-6 = will, 5 = will retain, etc.)

explanation: MQTT is the dominant IoT pub/sub protocol. CONNECT message types: 0x10 CONNECT, 0x20 CONNACK, 0x30 PUBLISH, 0x40 PUBACK, 0x82 SUBSCRIBE, 0xC0 PINGREQ. ConnectFlags carry username/password/will-message indicators. MQTT brokers exposed without auth (ConnectFlags missing username bit + accepting any clientID) are a common cloud-IoT misconfig, and shodan.io regularly catalogues thousands of them. Wire-format recognition is the precondition for spotting IoT-specific attack traffic.

fields_at_offsets.name: TPKT-version
fields_at_offsets.value: 0x03 (TPKT v3, used to wrap X.224 over TCP)

explanation: RDP wraps X.224 inside TPKT inside TCP/3389. The first packet (Connection Request) is plaintext and includes the 'mstshash=' username cookie - this is how exposed RDP servers leak the attempted username to anyone watching port 3389. RDP brute-force attacks generate floods of these on shadowserver / Censys honeypot data. The negotiation flags hint at what RDP security level is requested (legacy RDP, TLS, CredSSP). The canonical RDP-targeted detection is failed-connection bursts to port 3389.
